food.text: The Hittites, an Anatolian Indo-European people of the Bronze Age, left behind a good number of texts describing how they prepared food. They also had many laws stipulating how certain foods were to be prepared, cooked, and served.

The main ingredients of Hittite cuisine were dairy products, meat, grain products, and other natural products such as honey. It was a diet built on herds, fields, and the produce of the Anatolian land.
The Hittites loved bread. They had recipes for as many as 180 types of bread, in different shapes and with varying ingredients.

Hittite recipes were generally similar to those of contemporary civilizations, especially for meat and dairy dishes. They were unique in the plants they used, because Anatolia has its own specific vegetation.
The Hittites consumed wine on a regular basis, and it was used for religious festivals and rituals.

Adana, in southeast Turkey, was called Adaniya in Hittite and lay in the former Kizzuwadna region. It is famous for its kebabs, and studies suggest that Hittite cuisine already contained a strong element of meat skewer, or shish kebab.

art.text: At Alaca Höyük in Anatolia, fourteen shaft-grave "Royal Tombs" dating to 2850–2450 BC held the dead with folded legs, facing west, richly adorned with gold fibulae, diadems, belt buckles and repoussé gold-leaf figures. The heads and legs of bulls were placed on platforms beside them. These tombs date to the same period as the Royal Tombs of Ur.

In the Kura-Araxes culture of the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia, late burial kurgans held a wide assortment of metalworks, with larger, wealthier kurgans surrounded by smaller, less wealthy ones. This trend suggests the emergence of a marked social hierarchy.

In the Assyrian trading colonies called karum that operated in Anatolia from the 20th to the 18th centuries BC, merchants kept their Assyrian identity and customs. Yet the pottery and architecture built in these colonies followed local Anatolian styles.

At Kültepe, the ancient city of Kanesh, the palace known as the Waršama Sarayi, on the mound rather than the lower city, was built and later refurbished between about 1832 and 1779 BC. This dating comes from tree-ring analysis of its timber beams.

The Alaca Höyük tombs also contained seven metal figurines, four of bronze and three of silver. Pole finials shaped like bulls and stags, and other abstract forms, are often interpreted as solar symbols.

The Sphinx Gate at Alaca Höyük, surrounded by carved stone reliefs, dates to the Hittite period of the fourteenth century BC and marks the site's most distinctive standing monument. It served as the entrance to the settlement, built after the earlier Hattian era there.

German archaeologists excavating Alaca Höyük in the 1910s uncovered the Sphinx Gate, with its stone relief carvings, along with royal tombs dating to the third millennium BC. Further excavations starting in 1968 revealed considerable wealth and craftsmanship at the site even before the time of the Hittites.

In the final stage of the Kura-Araxes culture, collective burials were performed that included human sacrifices. The Martqopi period burial mounds on the left bank of the river Alazani, from the same final stage, are often 20 to 25 meters high and 200 to 300 meters in diameter. They contain especially rich artefacts, such as gold and silver jewelry.

The royal shaft tombs at Alaca Höyük were about 1.5 meters deep and sealed with wooden beams. They contained the dead with folded legs facing west, along with gold, bronze and silver objects. The heads and legs of bulls were placed on platforms in the tombs.

war.text: The Hittite Wars of Survival lasted from about 1400 BC to 1350 BC, pitting the Hittite Empire against neighbours including Arzawa, Kaška and Hayasa-Azzi. The Hittite capital Ḫattuša was sacked and their territory shrank to a small area around Šamuḫa. Much of the Hittite lands and cities were ravaged, with the grain-lands suffering particularly. The general and future king Šuppiluliuma then regained all the lost land and launched punitive expeditions.

The Late Bronze Age collapse of the late 13th to early 12th century BC was sudden, violent and culturally disruptive. By 1200 BC the Hittite Empire, which spanned Anatolia and the Levant, was already fragmenting under famine, plague and civil war, and then collapsed. The Hittite capital Hattusa was burned, though it may have been abandoned first. Karaoğlan, near present-day Ankara, was burned and its corpses were left unburied. The Middle Assyrian Empire and the New Kingdom of Egypt survived, though in weakened forms.

Under Arnuwanda I, the Kaška raided, seized and sacked many Hittite holy cities, including Tapikka, Šarišša and Šapinuwa. At one point they were some 100 km from the capital Ḫattuša. Arnuwanda had limited success pushing them out and even tried to pay them off diplomatically, but much of Ḫatti still remained under Kaška control. The Hittite Kingdom was a fragile structure, lacking the resources and manpower to respond effectively.

At Hattusa, archaeologists found a bronze sword during 1991 repair work, inscribed in Akkadian. It records that after Duthaliya the Great King shattered the Assuwa country, he dedicated these swords to the Storm-God, his lord.

The Hittite campaign against Arzawa was led by Šuppiluliuma because Tudḫaliya was growing ill. It is believed to have taken longer than the campaigns against Kaška and Hayasa-Azzi. In the 1350s BC Anzapahhadu of Arzawa routed a Hittite general named Himuili, but he was finally subdued by an incursion led by Šuppiluliuma himself.

In the early 2nd millennium BC the Lola culture of the North Caucasus came under increasing pressure from the Srubnaya culture, advancing from the Middle Volga region. By 1800 BC the Srubnaya had replaced the Lola population.

Under Arnuwanda I the Hittites could not firmly control Western Anatolia. The Indictment of Madduwatta records a nominally pro-Hittite vassal who, despite swearing fealty, kept stirring up trouble with neighbours such as Arzawa. This forced the Hittites to commit troops to the region.

A Mycenaean-style sword found at Hattusa bears an inscription suggesting it was taken from an Assuwan soldier and left as an offering to the Hittite storm god. It is circumstantial evidence that Ahhiyawans may have supported the Assuwa rebellion against the Hittites.

Tudhaliya and Mariya of Hayasa-Azzi had signed a treaty. When Mariya arrived in the Hittite land to pay tribute, Tudhaliya had Mariya executed for having flirted with some of Tudhaliya's palace women. The account comes from Richard H. Beal.

literature.text: Historians mark the end of Anatolian prehistory by the appearance of literacy and historical sources, around 2000 BCE. Before that, the region's story has to be pieced together from archaeology alone. Writing is what turns Anatolia's past into recorded history.

The oldest attested forms of any Semitic language date to the early to mid-3rd millennium BCE, in the Early Bronze Age. They come from Mesopotamia, the northwest Levant and southeast Anatolia, so this corner of Anatolia was part of the earliest Semitic-language record.

The Alaksandu Treaty was made between a Wilusan king named Alaksandu and the Hittite king Muwatalli II. Among the gods guaranteeing the treaty on Wilusa's behalf is Apaliunas, a name identified with Apollo.

The name of the Anatolian kingdom of Ishuwa is not known until the literate period of the second millennium BC. Few written sources from inside Ishuwa have been found, so most of what we know comes from Hittite texts written by its western neighbour.

The city of Wilusa, identified with Troy, first appears in the record around 1400 BC. It was one of twenty-two states of the Assuwa Confederation that tried to oppose the Hittites. The Annals of Tudhaliya I/II give a detailed account of the Assuwans' defeat.

Attarsiya was a 15th to 14th century BC military leader who was probably Greek. He conducted the first recorded Mycenaean military activity on the Anatolian mainland, and his activities are known from the Hittite archives of c. 1400 BC.

The Alaksandu Treaty required Wilusa to provide timely intelligence about anti-Hittite activity, and soldiers for military expeditions. Some evidence suggests Muwatalli II invoked the soldier clause, since Wilusan troops appear to have served in the Hittite army at the Battle of Kadesh.

King Walmu of Wiluša is known from only one text, the Milawata letter. It reports that he had been deposed and discusses the Hittite Empire's intent to reinstall him. The letter does not say how he lost his throne or who was responsible.

The Annals of Mursili II recount how the Hittite king besieged the capital of the Seha River Land around 1320 BC. He was on the verge of destroying it when he accepted a last-minute plea for mercy from King Manapa-Tarhunta's own mother, delivered right outside the city gates.

The letter from Millawata (Miletus) states that Walmu sought political asylum from Tarkasnawa, his suzerain in the kingdom of Mira. King Tudhaliya IV seems to have urged Tarkasnawa to send Walmu to the Hittite Kingdom so he could be put back on his throne.

The Manapa-Tarhunta letter records a second plea for mercy from the Seha River Land's king, this time addressed to Mursili II. Manapa-Tarhunta had failed to provide the Hittite king with timely military support.

science.text: Bronze metallurgy spread to Anatolia from the Transcaucasian Kura-Araxes culture in the late 4th millennium BCE. Its arrival marked the beginning of the Bronze Age in the region.

Bronze Age Anatolia was well endowed with copper ores. Yet there is no trace so far of substantial workings of the tin needed to make bronze. As far as is known, the Akkadian Empire's interest in the region was in exporting various materials for manufacturing.
In Anatolia and the Caucasus, the Iron Age began around 1300 BC. In the ancient Near East, this transition happened at the same time as the Late Bronze Age collapse, during the 12th century BC.

After 3000 BC, Kura–Araxes sites used far more metal objects, and the range of copper alloys grew. Some copper objects contained an arsenical component of up to 25%, giving them a shiny greyish, silvery colour. It is quite possible these alloys were meant to imitate silver.

Bronze metallurgy spread to Anatolia from the Transcaucasian Kura-Araxes culture, marking the start of the Bronze Age there. Anatolia was well endowed with copper ores, but there is no trace yet of substantial workings of the tin needed to make bronze in Bronze-Age Anatolia.

In the early second millennium BC, Old Assyrian merchants brought tin and textiles into Anatolia. They took silver and other commodities in return. This network connected central Anatolian cities with northern Mesopotamia.

Thousands of cuneiform tablets recovered at Kanesh record contracts, loans, caravan transport, taxation, family businesses and partnerships. They involved both Assyrian merchants and local Anatolians. Kanesh was the centre of a network of Assyrian trading colonies.

A depiction of a two-wheeled vehicle with four-spoked wheels is known from Kültepe in Central Anatolia, dating from about 1900 BC. It appears at the same time as steppe horses in the region. Chariot wheels from the Sintashta and Andronovo cultures near the Urals had more than four spokes.

Iron fragments found in Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük date to 2200 to 2000 BC. One study says iron implements were made in Central Anatolia in very limited quantities about 1800 BC. During the Neo-Hittite Empire (c. 1400 to 1200 BC) they were in general use by elites, though not by commoners.

Recent evidence suggests that the collapse of Hittite Anatolia, Mycenaean Greece and the Levant may have been worsened by disease. An early, now-extinct strain of bubonic plague may have been brought from central Asia by the Sea Peoples or other migrating groups.

politics.text: The Hittites built one of the first major civilizations of the Bronze Age in West Asia. At its peak in the mid-14th century BC under Šuppiluliuma I, their empire, centered on Hattusa, covered most of Anatolia and parts of northern Syria and Upper Mesopotamia.

Between the 15th and 13th centuries BC, the Hittites were the most dominant powers of the Near East. They came into conflict with the New Kingdom of Egypt, the Middle Assyrian Empire and the Empire of Mitanni.

Around 1200 BC the palace economy of Anatolia, the Aegean and Mycenaean Greece disintegrated in the Late Bronze Age collapse. The Hittite Empire, which spanned Anatolia and the Levant, collapsed, while the Middle Assyrian Empire and the New Kingdom of Egypt survived in weakened forms.

Under the Old Hittite Kingdom, before 1400 BC, the king was not seen as a living god like the pharaohs of Egypt, but as a first among equals. Only from 1400 BC until 1200 BC did the kingship become more centralized and powerful.
In 1700 BC, King Anitta of Kussar burned Hattush to the ground after overthrowing King Piyushti. He placed a curse on the site and set up his capital at Kanesh, about 160 km to the southeast.

The Hittite Empire was at its height in the 14th century BCE. Kizzuwatna in southern Anatolia controlled the region separating Hatti from Syria and so greatly affected trade routes, and peace was kept through treaties that established boundaries of control.

The Late Bronze Age collapse brought down the Hittite Empire, which had spanned Anatolia and the Levant. The Middle Assyrian Empire and the New Kingdom of Egypt survived in weakened forms, while the Phoenicians gained autonomy as Egyptian and Assyrian military presence waned.

In the Old Hittite Kingdom the succession was not legally fixed, enabling "War of the Roses"-style rivalries between northern and southern branches of the royal family. After Mursili I was assassinated by his brother-in-law Hantili I, the kingdom was plunged into chaos: Hantili's wife Harapsili and her son were murdered, other royal family members were killed by Zidanta I, and Zidanta was then murdered by his own son, Ammuna. This was one factor in a repeating pattern of expansion under strong kings and contraction under weaker ones.
King Hattusili I, who reigned from 1586 to 1556 BC, moved his capital back to Hattusha from Neša (Kanesh). Hattusha had become a Hittite centre by the second half of the 17th century BC.

By the 13th century BC Assyria was expanding northwest at the expense of the Hittites. Its expansion reached its height under Tukulti-Ninurta I, who reigned from 1244 to 1208 BC, after which it was weakened by internal dissent.

At the beginning of the 12th century BCE, Wilusa (Troy) was destroyed and the Hittite New Kingdom suffered a sudden devastating attack from the Kaskas, who occupied the coasts around the Black Sea and joined with the Mysians. They proceeded to destroy almost all Hittite sites, and Hatti, Arzawa, Alashiya, Ugarit and Alalakh were destroyed too. Hattusa, the Hittite capital, was completely destroyed, though the attackers were finally defeated by the Assyrians beyond the southern borders near the Tigris. Later Neo-Hittite rulers deliberately tied their titles and imagery to the Hittite Empire.

Kizzuwatna was not fully taken over until the reign of the Hittite king Šuppiluliuma II. Even then, the Hittites preserved their cultural accomplishments in Kummanni and Lazawantiya, north of Cilicia.

philosophy.text: Puduhepa, queen of the Hittite king Hattusili III, came from Kizzuwatna, where she had been a priestess. The kingdom's pantheon was integrated into the Hittite one. Its goddess Hebat became very important in Hittite religion towards the end of the 13th century BC.
In Hittite texts, pieces of the Luwian language often appear in magic rituals meant to bring rain or heal the sick. These rituals give an important role to the goddess Kamrusepa.
The Hattians lived in monarchical city-states in central Anatolia. These states were ruled as theocratic kingdoms or principalities, so religious and political authority were tied together.

Luwian religion is usually split into a Bronze Age period and an Iron Age period. In the Bronze Age the Luwians lived under Hittite control. A hieroglyphic script existed then, yet only a few religious texts of the Luwians are known from that time.

Luwian religion was strongly affected by foreign influence, so it cannot be clearly separated from neighbouring Syrian and Hurrian religion. Even so, its Indo-European element was stronger than in the neighbouring Hittite religion.

The Palaic storm god had a temple in the Hittite capital Ḫattuša. Ritual texts in cuneiform from that temple are how the Palaic religion is known. The cult of Palaic deities continued there even after contacts between the Hittites and Pala had disappeared.

The typical Luwian gods, always worshipped, were Tarhunt, Tiwad, Arma, Runtiya and Šanta. A Hurrian element, with Syrian and Babylonian influences, became visible later. It brought deities such as Iya, Hipatu, Šaruma, Alanzu and Šauska.

Unlike the Hittite religion, the Luwian religion was not significantly influenced by Hattian religion. This sets the two neighbouring belief systems apart, even though both existed under the Hittites.
It has been speculated that Palaic-speakers were never literate. On that view, Hittite scribes used a syllabary to incorporate the Palaic traditions into the Hittite state cult.

Local Luwian cults are also attested in Hittite texts, such as that of Ḫuwaššanna of Ḫubišna, modern Ereğli in Konya. The pantheon of the city of Ištanuwa, thought to lie in the area of the Sakarya River, belongs to the Luwian religious zone.

culture.text: The Kura–Araxes culture existed from about 4000 BC until about 2000 BC. It spread north in the Caucasus by 3000 BC. It eventually covered an area about 1,000 km by 500 km, including modern Armenia, eastern Georgia, Azerbaijan, northwestern Iran and eastern Turkey.

The Trialeti-Vanadzor culture is named after the Trialeti region in Georgia and the city of Vanadzor in Armenia. It flourished between the late 3rd and early 2nd millennium BCE in the territories of the earlier Kura–Araxes culture. Its elite were entombed in large, richly furnished kurgans, some containing four-wheeled carts and gold objects, and its burial practices included cremation and ritual animal sacrifices.

The Luwians were an Indo-European people of Asia Minor whose religion is detectable from the Bronze Age. During that time they were under Hittite control. A hieroglyphic script existed for writing Luwian, but only a few religious texts from the Bronze Age are known.

The Kura–Araxes culture lasted from about 4000 BC until about 2000 BC and covered an area of about 1,000 km by 500 km. Its lands included northwestern Iran, along with Armenia, eastern Georgia, Azerbaijan and eastern Turkey. It was characterized by an agricultural sedentary economy.

In the 3rd millennium BC, the Martqopi period burial mounds marked the final stage of the Kura–Araxes culture and were remarkable for their wealth. Those on the left bank of the river Alazani are often 20–25 meters high and 200–300 meters across, and held gold and silver jewelry. The article also says that in the final stage of this civilization, collective burials were performed which included human sacrifices.

Shengavit Settlement, in the present-day Yerevan area in Armenia, was a prominent Kura–Araxes site. It was inhabited from about 3200 BC cal to 2500 BC cal. The town covered six hectares, which is large for Kura-Araxes sites.

Boris Kuftin discovered and named the Trialeti culture in the late 1930s. Gamkrelidze and Ivanov later identified parallels between Indo-European burial customs and the kurgan tombs characteristic of Trialeti-Vanadzor sites.

Studies increasingly see the Trialeti-Vanadzor culture as an early Proto-Armenian cultural horizon. It eventually evolved into the Lchashen–Metsamor culture. It has also been suggested as a cultural precursor to the Hayasa-Azzi confederation mentioned in Hittite records.

The earliest evidence of the Luwians comes from the Old Assyrian archive of traders at the Karum of Kaneš, around 1900 BC. Some people there bore clearly Luwian names containing gods' names. These names indicate that Šanta and Runtiya were worshipped as deities.

Tarhunt, Tiwad, Arma, Runtiya and Šanta are named as the typical Luwian gods, always worshipped. Hurrian influence, with deities like Iya, Hipatu, Šaruma, Alanzu and Šauska, became visible later. Unlike the Hittites, the Luwians were not significantly influenced by Hattian religion.
